nv_front_corridor.blurb: Front Corridor is a narrow sandstone slot at the Sandstone Quarry in Red Rock, a couple of minutes on foot from the lot. It holds about twenty routes, nearly all of them bolted, with a few trad lines. The grades lean hard: a handful in the 5.9 to 5.10 range, then a thick middle of 5.11s and a short run of 5.12 and 5.13 on the steeper side. The side walls are mostly shaded, with sun reaching in for a short while around midday, which suits warmer days. Expect crimpy Red Rock face climbing, and on the more adventurous lines some brittle rock. It is a good stop for climbers working through the 5.11 grades.

nv_black_wall_aka_happy_acres.blurb: Black Wall, also known as Happy Acres, is a sandstone wall in Calico Basin on the Red Rock side of Las Vegas, sitting roughly halfway up the canyon beyond the main crags. Most lines here run two or three pitches, with a blend of bolted and traditional climbing plus a few single-pitch options and one top rope. The grades are friendly: mostly 5.7 to 5.10, with just one 5.11. The face looks northeast, so it picks up a little early sun and then sits in shade for the rest of the day, which makes it a decent pick when the weather is warm. The hike in is steeper than at the roadside walls.

nv_cactus_massacre.blurb: Cactus Massacre is a steep grey sandstone wall at the First Pullout (Calico I) in Red Rock, west of Las Vegas. Nearly everything here is bolted, with only a couple of trad lines. The grades span a wide range: a pair of very easy routes, a group of 5.7 to 5.9, then a solid core of 5.10 and 5.11 with a couple of 5.12s at the top end. That mix makes it useful for parties with different abilities. The wall gets sun from mid-morning onward, so it is better on cool days. The approach drops down from the lot past a neighbouring cliff and crosses a gully, taking roughly ten minutes.

nv_water_world.blurb: Water World is a wall of sharp grey limestone in Box Canyon, a tight slot canyon west of Las Vegas in the La Madre area. All of its roughly twenty routes are bolted sport lines, about 30 to 60 feet tall. Grades are centred on 5.10, with a few easier ones at 5.8 and 5.9 and a handful of 5.11s, so it suits climbers cruising the middle grades. Getting here is the real effort: the approach is a long hike on a dirt and gravel road system followed by a walk up the wash to the point where it splits into two canyons, with the wall on the west side. Plan a full day and carry plenty of water.

nv_jimbo_rocks.blurb: Jimbo Rocks is a cluster of boulders in the lower stretch of Keyhole Canyon in the Eldorado Mountains of southern Nevada, just inside the canyon mouth. Nearly all of the problems are boulders, with one aid line, and the range runs from beginner-friendly slabs and easy faces up to a couple of hard testpieces, with most problems between VB and V5. Features include arêtes, a slab, a traverse over a chockstone and a small cave with a roof line and an unfinished project. It is a short walk from the wash and is often called the best warm-up spot in the lower canyon, though sun exposure is not well documented.

nv_classic_rock_right_sw.blurb: Classic Rock Right is the southwest section of Classic Rock Wall, a sandstone crag tucked into a small canyon below the First Pullout (Calico I) in Red Rock. About twenty routes are here, nearly all bolted, plus a single top rope and one trad line. The grades center on the 5.8 to 5.11 band, with a few 5.7s at the low end and just two climbs harder than 5.11, so intermediates will find plenty to do. Climbing ranges from technical slab to pumpy, huecoed faces. The canyon setting blocks most wind, and the crag is a popular pick for families. It is about a five minute walk from the lot via a staircase.

nv_the_pier.blurb: The Pier is a short, shady sandstone crag in the Sandstone Quarry zone of Red Rock, a few minutes down a marked trail from the lot. Nearly everything here is bolted, mostly at 5.11 and 5.12, with a few 5.13s, one easier 5.9, and two boulder problems. The wall faces close to north, stays shaded for most of the season with just a sliver of late-evening light on long spring days, so it works well when other crags are baking. Expect typical Red Rock style: crimpy, slightly overhanging faces broken up by some huecos and cracks. A few routes are short or a bit less polished than their neighbours.
